title: As Harvard launches course with AI professors, what is the future of teaching in India?
key_facts: Commentary by Angshuman Kar, Professor of English at The University of Burdwan, on an eight-week online entrepreneurship bootcamp from Harvard Business School called HBS Foundry.

Participants pitch start-up ideas to an AI avatar modelled on a real professor; the programme costs $699 (roughly Rs 67,000) and combines Harvard course material, AI agents trained on faculty expertise, a community of entrepreneurs and simulated video conversations with AI avatars.
The aim is to reach far more people than the roughly 900 students the business school admits each year; the Harvard details are taken from a New York Times report, not from Scroll's own reporting.
Katharina Rings, director of HBS Foundry, told the New York Times that in trial runs users became more interested when chatbot advisors were given the appearance of a professor.

Kar asks whether AI professors could ease India's shortage of quality teachers, citing a Tata Institute of Social Sciences survey of schools in 10 states that found a shortage of maths and science teachers and more multi-grade classrooms in rural government schools.

Kar warns that a new 'AI divide' could open between students with internet, devices, electricity and digital skills and those without, and that a lack of good AI content in Indian languages could widen inequality with English-speaking students.
Kar argues the warmth, trust and personal connection between teacher and student are hard to reproduce, and that teachers may need to become mentors and facilitators.
HBS Foundry professor Thomas Eisenmann told the New York Times that students 'love AI' but that it 'keeps coming back to humanity'.
quote_evidence: An eight-week online entrepreneurship bootcamp launched by Harvard Business School lets participants pitch a start-up idea to an artificial-intelligence avatar modelled on a real professor.
The HBS Foundry programme, designed to train aspiring entrepreneurs, costs $699, or roughly Rs 67,000.
Students from any part of the country could have the opportunity to interact with an AI avatar created by a teacher whose direct teaching they would otherwise have no access to.
why_it_matters_hint: A top business school is selling teaching delivered partly by AI copies of its professors, which prompts the question whether the same model could stretch scarce teachers in India, and who would be left out.
event_date: Not stated; the HBS Foundry launch and the New York Times report it rests on are undated in the column (Scroll column published 12 Oct 2026).
notes: Opinion column, not a news report: the Harvard facts are second-hand from the New York Times, which is named but not linked; the launch date of the programme is not given. Read in full from the AMP page.
